4.8 Behavioral Finance

Prospect theory

Section titled “Prospect theory”

The expected utility theory of 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty assumes that people decide by the utility of final wealth, and that risk aversion comes from the concavity of the utility function. Some patterns in experiments and in actual behavior do not fit it. The prospect theory of Kahneman and Tversky (1979) describes how people actually choose under risk with three features:

  • Reference point: people judge gains and losses relative to some reference point (the purchase price, the status quo, an expectation), not the level of final wealth.
  • Loss aversion: a loss hurts a little more than twice as much as a gain of the same size pleases.
  • Diminishing sensitivity: the larger the gain or loss, the weaker the feeling of each extra dollar. So the value function is concave for gains (risk averse when facing gains) and convex for losses (willing to take risks when facing losses).

The value function estimated by Tversky and Kahneman (1992) is

v(x)={xa,x≥0−λ(−x)a,x<0a≈0.88, λ≈2.25v(x) = \begin{cases} x^{a}, & x \ge 0 \\ -\lambda(-x)^{a}, & x < 0 \end{cases} \qquad a \approx 0.88,\ \lambda \approx 2.25v(x)={xa,−λ(−x)a,​x≥0x<0​a≈0.88, λ≈2.25

In addition, people give too much weight to events with small probabilities: this can explain why people buy both lottery tickets and insurance, and why stocks that, like lotteries, have a small chance of a huge gain tend to be overpriced and to earn low average returns.

Check C1
In Figure 1-1, keep a = 0.88 and raise the loss aversion λ from 1 to 2.25. The value of a gamble with a 50% chance to win 100 dollars and a 50% chance to lose 100:
Does λ magnify the value on the loss side or the gain side?
Look at the formula: does λ multiply all losses or only large ones?
With λ = 1 and the same a on both sides, winning 100 and losing 100 have values of the same size. What is the gamble's value then?

Convexity on the loss side has a direct consequence: when someone who is already losing must choose between “a sure loss” and “a chance to win it back or to lose more”, which do they choose?

Check C2
By prospect theory, an investor who is already losing faces two choices: a sure further loss of 50 dollars, or a 50% chance of losing 100 more and a 50% chance of losing nothing more. He is more likely to:
In prospect theory, is the value function concave or convex on the loss side? What does convexity imply about choices under risk?
The expected values are equal, but the value function is not a straight line. Which is smaller, v(−50)v(-50)v(−50) or 0.5 v(−100)0.5\,v(-100)0.5v(−100)?
What does prospect theory judge, final wealth or changes relative to a reference point?

Expected utility theory has trouble explaining why people turn down small favorable gambles: for someone with wealth of a few hundred thousand dollars, the utility function is almost a straight line over a few hundred dollars, so by expected utility they should be close to risk neutral (Rabin, 2000). Prospect theory explains this behavior by loss aversion around the reference point (Exercises Question 1).

Common biases

Section titled “Common biases”
  • Overconfidence: overrating the accuracy of one’s own knowledge and judgment. Barber and Odean (2000) studied about 66,000 household accounts at a US discount broker in 1991–1996; the fifth of households that traded most earned about 11.4% a year net, while the market earned about 17.9%.
  • Disposition effect: a tendency to sell winning stocks too early and to hold losing stocks too long (Shefrin and Statman, 1985). Odean (1998) found that the winners investors sold went on, over the next year, to do better on average than the losers they kept. The purchase price is a reference point, and selling a loser means “admitting” the loss.
  • Mental accounting: putting money into separate “accounts” and treating each on its own (Thaler, 1985), for example treating dividends as “income” that can be spent while being unwilling to sell shares, or taking bolder risks with money that was won. Money is interchangeable, and deciding account by account ignores the whole.
  • Herding: following what others do instead of judging from one’s own information. Others’ actions may contain information, but when everyone follows, prices can drift further and further from fundamentals.

There are also anchoring (relying too much on an initial number when estimating), limited attention (underreacting to information that is not prominent) and extrapolating past trends. These biases can explain some of the anomalies in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis: limited attention and conservatism fit post-earnings-announcement drift, and extrapolation and overreaction fit long-run reversal.

Check C3
In a taxable account, the disposition effect (a tendency to sell winning stocks and keep losing ones) usually helps the investor's tax bill.
Think: does selling a winner realize a capital gain or a capital loss? What does a realized capital loss do to taxes?
Check C4
Barber and Odean (2000) found that the households that traded most had the lowest net returns. The main reason is:
The market rose a lot in 1991–1996. If they had simply taken more risk, should their returns have been higher or lower?
If they had used inside information, should their returns have been higher or lower?
Where did the main difference come from, trading costs and the results of stock picking, or manipulation by the broker?

Limits to arbitrage

Section titled “Limits to arbitrage”

Supporters of efficient markets argue that even if many investors are biased, rational arbitrageurs will buy undervalued assets and short overvalued ones, pushing prices back. Behavioral finance answers that arbitrage is risky and costly, so mispricing can last a long time. These are the limits to arbitrage:

  • Fundamental risk: an undervalued stock has no perfect substitute, and the assets used to hedge cannot remove all the risk (4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta).
  • Noise trader risk: the investors who push prices away from value may become even more extreme in the short run, so the gap widens before it narrows (De Long, Shleifer, Summers and Waldmann, 1990).
  • Implementation costs: shorting requires borrowing shares and paying fees, and the shares may be recalled; some assets are very hard to short.
  • Funding: most arbitrageurs manage other people’s money. When the gap widens, the arbitrage position loses money, investors may withdraw, and arbitrageurs are forced to close at the worst moment (Shleifer and Vishny, 1997).

A classic example is Royal Dutch and Shell Transport. The two companies shared the same cash flows in a fixed ratio of 60:40, so their price ratio should in theory have been constant; in fact it departed from parity for long periods: Royal Dutch was at times about 35% below parity and at other times about 15% above it (Froot and Dabora, 1999).

Check C5
Two stocks represent fixed shares of the same cash flows, and their price ratio has moved 10% away from its theoretical value. Which best explains why arbitrageurs do not remove the gap at once?
The question says they represent fixed shares of the same cash flows.
If the ratio eventually returns to its theoretical value, does buying the cheap one and shorting the dear one make money in the end?
The gap can be observed directly from the two prices. Does it not exist?

What it means for investors

Section titled “What it means for investors”

For individual investors, the most direct use of behavioral finance is often not finding other people’s mistakes but avoiding one’s own:

  • The more often one trades, the more overconfidence costs; a diversified portfolio with low turnover reduces such losses.
  • Decide whether to sell by future prospects, not by the purchase price, and in a taxable account consider taxes as well (Exercises Question 2, 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US)).
  • Write an investment plan and rebalancing rules in advance (6.7 Asset Allocation), so as to act less on emotion when markets rise or fall sharply.
  • Judge risk at the level of the whole portfolio, not one stock or one account at a time; checking the account often makes one feel more losses.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Prospect theory: gains and losses relative to a reference point; loss aversion (λ about 2.25); concave for gains and convex for losses; overweighting of small probabilities.
  • Common biases: overconfidence, the disposition effect, mental accounting, herding, anchoring, limited attention, extrapolation; they can explain some anomalies.
  • Limits to arbitrage: fundamental risk, noise trader risk, implementation costs and funding allow mispricing to last.
  • For individual investors, using rules and diversification to reduce one’s own biases is more realistic than exploiting others’ biases.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A person has wealth of 100,000 dollars. He is offered a gamble with a 50% chance to win 110 dollars and a 50% chance to lose 100 dollars. He turns it down.
(a) Using the Tversky–Kahneman value function (a=0.88a = 0.88a=0.88, λ=2.25\lambda = 2.25λ=2.25, with the status quo as the reference point), compute the value of the gamble. With the loss still 100 dollars, how large must the win be for him to accept?
(b) A colleague says: "He turned down a gamble with a positive expected value, so his relative risk aversion must be very high (by the CRRA utility of 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty), and he should hold almost no stocks." Check with log utility u(W)=ln⁡Wu(W) = \ln Wu(W)=lnW (relative risk aversion 1) whether he would accept the gamble, and evaluate the colleague's statement.
Question 2
Two years ago an investor bought 50,000 dollars each of stocks A and B. A is now worth 65,000 dollars and B 35,000 dollars. He needs 10,000 dollars in cash and plans to sell 10,000 dollars of A: "A made money, so I'll lock in the profit; I'll sell B once it climbs back to what I paid." His views on the two stocks' futures are the same. Assume a long-term capital gains tax rate of 15%, and that realized capital losses can offset his other capital gains this year.
(a) Selling 10,000 dollars of A, how much tax does he pay on the realized gain? If he sold 10,000 dollars of B instead, how much tax would the realized loss save?
(b) Evaluate his reasoning. What is wrong with "waiting for it to climb back to what I paid"?
Question 3
Stocks X and Y represent identical claims on the same cash flows, so in theory their prices should be equal; X is now 10% more expensive than Y. An arbitrage fund with 10 million dollars of capital buys 50 million dollars of Y and shorts 50 million dollars of X. For simplicity, each percentage point of change in the gap changes the position's value by about 1% of 50 million dollars.
(a) If the gap eventually returns to 0, what is the fund's return on capital? If the gap first widens to 20%, how much does the fund lose (in millions of dollars), and what share of its capital is that?
(b) An analyst says: "Mispricing must be removed by arbitrage, and an arbitrageur who is right about the direction is sure to make money." Using (a), evaluate this statement. What changes if the fund uses only 1 times leverage (10 million dollars long and 10 million short)?
Question 4
A popular stock trades at 200 times next year's expected earnings. The company expects to pay out 50% of its earnings as dividends, and investors require a return of 9%.
(a) By the Gordon growth model (3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models), what permanent dividend growth rate does this price imply? Compared with long-run nominal economic growth (about 4% to 5%), is this assumption reasonable?
(b) A friend says: "I know it's expensive, but everyone is buying, so the price will keep rising. I just need to sell a little earlier than everyone else." Evaluate this statement. Why might investors who see that it is expensive still not short it?
